Abstract
Recommender systems are central to debates over whether digital platforms fragment public discourse or sustain exposure to diverse information, yet empirical findings remain heterogeneous. This study examines how filter bubbles, echo chambers, and polarization are conceptualized and operationalized in recommender-system research and integrates evidence across algorithmic, behavioral, relational, and outcome levels. A systematic review of 60 studies published between 2020 and 2025, conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA, informs the development of the Platform-Mediated Polarization Framework (PMPF). Extending the recursive logic of Reinforcing Spirals Theory to computationally adaptive recommender environments, PMPF conceptualizes recursive exposure production as a process through which behavioral responses to prior exposure may be incorporated into subsequent ranking and personalization. Evidence was more extensive and direct for recommender-mediated structuring and differentiation of informational exposure than for attitudinal or ideological polarization. Evidence for polarization was more heterogeneous, suggesting that such outcomes are contingent on behavioral, relational, informational, and contextual processes. Direct evidence of recursive feedback was limited to a subset of studies, while others examined component processes or addressed feedback conceptually. The evidence therefore does not support a uniform relationship between recommender systems and polarization. Instead, PMPF integrates these patterns within a system-level framewo

4. Discussion
Based on the review, it appears that the relation between recommender systems and polarization is not a consistent one but rather dependent on certain conditions. In particular, the direct evidence in this context is found in the reviewed articles concerning exposure conditions mediated by recommender systems. The evidence of recursive relations and polarization as a consequence is somewhat inconsistent and indirect, and evidence of behavior and relational aspects of the relation are even less present and consistent. It suggests that the review demonstrates a hierarchical structure, with the support becoming increasingly weaker moving from exposure conditions to recursive relations and attitudinal outcomes.
This evidentiary hierarchy is the starting point for the Platform-Mediated Polarization Framework (PMPF). PMPF is not supposed to be an alternative to already established theories of media selection, reinforcement, and platform influence. An important theoretical base for the recursive relations in recommender systems is provided by Reinforcing Spirals Theory (RST), which explains how there can be reciprocal relations between media selection, media use, and user dispositions (
Slater, 2007
,
2015
). Thus, PMPF adds the concept of computational adaptability to RST and provides more detail on how user behaviors after previous exposures can become machine-readable inputs and influence recommender systems’ algorithms. Selective-exposure research provides an explanation of behavioral selection, echo-chamber theory highlights the relational aspects such as

[... bounded source excerpt ...]

sal model but as a system-level theoretical framework generating testable hypotheses about recursive exposure pathways.
5. Conclusion
In summary, this review aimed to examine whether algorithmically organized recommendation contributes to common informational conditions or fragmentation and polarization. Synthesis of 60 studies shows that there is no simple answer either in terms of consensus or conflict. The evidence is more extensive and more direct in relation to informational exposure, while evidence regarding recursive relationships and polarization is more varied. Therefore, recommender systems should be considered as socio-technologies that configure the conditions of communication, but not mechanisms producing polarization per se. One of the implications of the review is that exposure conditions and polarization outcomes should be treated separately. Recommendation can influence the visibility, diversity, and distribution of recommended content, and, in some cases, the exposure of users to information. However, differences in exposure cannot be considered as polarization itself. Filter bubbles indicate certain patterns of narrowed or concentrated exposure; echo chambers concern the relations based on homophily, clustering, and social reinforcement; and polarization indicates the structured divergence in attitudes, affective orientations, perception, or ideology. In this sense, the evidence collected does not suggest the inevitability of the chain in which recommendation produces filter bubbles and then echo chambers and, finally, polarization.
On the contrary, the key theoretical contribution of the study to the field is the Platform-Mediated Polarization Framework (PMPF). PMPF

Recommender systems as recursive exposure systems in the production of polarization\", \"abstract\": null, \"doi\": null, \"pmid\": \"PMC13662418\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13662418\", \"source\": \"PMC\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13662418/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13662418/pdf/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13662418\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13662418?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Unpacking the dual-path trust mechanism driving students' continuance intention toward campus GenAI: a hybrid SEM-machine learning approach within the S-O-R framework.\", \"abstract\": \"As generative artificial intelligence agents become embedded in higher education, understanding students' continuance intention (CUI) is critical. To address the underexplored mechanisms regarding how campus AI environments are associated with user trust, this study adopts the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework to investigate a dual-path trust mechanism: AI System-like Trust (AST) and AI Human-like Trust (AHT). Through a hybrid methodology combining Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and non-parametric Random Forest classification, this study analyzes university students' CUI toward campus GenAI. The findings demonstrate that Information Quality (IQ) and Service Quality (SQ) are positively associated with both AST and AHT pathways. Conversely, Facilitating Conditions (FC) and Performance Expectancy (PE) do not exhibit independent linear associations within the simultaneous structural estimation. Rather than indicating an empirical absence of functional value, this configuration uncovers a holistic evaluation mechanism among digital natives, where basic functional affordances operate as baseline hygiene constraints whose variance is subsumed by quality attributes. Notably, while both AST and AHT exert concurrently significant linear driving forces on CUI within the structural path framework, the exploratory machine learning analysis clarifies that under recursive partitioning, AHT exhibits a higher relative predictive weight. Furthermore, a localized asymmetry operates within the linear mediation channels, where SQ selectively mobilizes AHT over AST to drive continuous usage. Post-hoc inspections imply that PE operates through a non-linear threshold dynamic, transitioning into an active predictive catalyst primarily within the positive spectrum of user perception. Our study contributes to campus AI services evaluation by highlighting that within the contemporary GenAI ecosystem, students' evaluative focus prioritizes relational and epistemic quality over functional accessibility. Campus application administrators and developers are advised to prioritize content rigor and responsive, empathetic interaction design to cultivate the relational trust relevant for sustained engagement.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1903629\", \"pmid\": \"42539515\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13423894\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1903629\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13423894\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13423894?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Closing the Loop on the Cocktail Party Effect: From Attention Decoding to Neuro-Steered Selective Hearing.\", \"abstract\": \"Selective hearing in multi-talker environments remains a central challenge for assistive listening technologies: conventional devices improve audibility but cannot infer which talker the listener intends to follow. This Perspective examines the emerging transition from auditory attention decoding to neuro-steered selective hearing. We argue that a recent real-time intracranial proof-of-principle study marks an important inflection point in this transition, because it shows, under high-fidelity recordings from neurosurgical patients and in controlled two-talker conditions, that decoded neural attention can be coupled online to relative-gain control, thereby improving speech perception and reducing listening effort within that experimental setting. Building on this proof of principle, we argue that the field should move beyond offline decoding accuracy as its primary benchmark and instead treat neuro-steered hearing as a closed-loop translational problem linking neural inference, acoustic scene analysis, and control policy. From this perspective, future benchmarks should integrate device-level control metrics, including latency, effective switch time, false-switch rate and recovery after erroneous updates, with listener-centered outcomes such as speech intelligibility, listening effort, user preference and everyday benefit. Accordingly, we outline a staged roadmap for electroencephalography-based systems, from controlled two-speaker paradigms to scene-aware control and ultimately wearable real-world implementations. We also discuss the complementary roles of magnetoencephalography, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, and functional magnetic resonance imaging in defining the neural mechanisms and design constraints of future systems. Overall, this Perspective frames neuro-steered selective hearing as a systems-level research pathway for evaluating whether neural attention signals can be translated into practical assistive listening technologies.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/biology15141148\", \"pmid\": \"42510695\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13406005\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/biology15141148\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13406005\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13406005?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Closing the Empirical Loop: Autonomous AI Agents Conduct End-to-end Research With Human Participants.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence systems are transforming scientific discovery by accelerating specific research tasks, from protein structure prediction to materials design, yet remain confined to narrow domains requiring substantial human oversight. Exponential growth of scientific literature and increasing domain specialization constrain researchers' capacity to synthesize knowledge across disciplines and develop unifying theories, motivating exploration of general-purpose AI systems for science. Here we show that a domain-agnostic, agentic AI Scientist system can independently navigate the scientific workflow -from hypothesis generation through data collection to manuscript preparation. The system autonomously designed and executed three psychological studies on visual working memory, mental rotation, and imagery vividness, executed online data collection with 288 participants, developed analysis pipelines through 8h+ continuous coding sessions, and produced completed manuscripts. The results demonstrate the capability of AI scientific discovery pipelines to conduct research with theoretical reasoning and methodological rigor comparable to experienced researchers, though with limitations in conceptual nuance and theoretical interpretation. This is a step toward embodied AI that can test hypotheses through real-world experiments, accelerating discovery by autonomously exploring regions of scientific space that human cognitive and resource constraints might otherwise leave unexplored. It raises important questions about the nature of scientific understanding and attribution of scientific credit.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.76675\", \"pmid\": \"42734488\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13573717\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.76675\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13573717\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13573717?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "507383804c10aa27042e7fe706d1ff91f10d4c929e74755db0dba77d148444e0", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1903629", "doi:10.3390/biology15141148", "doi:10.1002/advs.76675", "pmc:PMC13662418", "pmc:PMC13423894", "pmc:PMC13406005", "pmc:PMC13573717"], "source_candidates": ["https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13662418/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13662418/pdf/?tool=EBI", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13662418", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13662418?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1903629", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13423894", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13423894?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3390/biology15141148"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
